pairs.source_text: Summa itaque rerum diuisio in duos articulos diducitur: nam aliae sunt diuini iuris, aliae humani.
pairs.question: Quae est summa rerum divisio secundum Gaium?
pairs.answer: Res aliae divini iuris sunt, aliae humani.
pairs.question_en: What is the highest division of things according to Gaius?
pairs.answer_en: Some things are of divine law, others of human law.
pairs.derivation: Gaius's famous summa divisio rerum opening the law of things: things are either divini iuris or humani iuris. Closed-book foundational maxim, anchored to Gaius + ius rerum, short two-part answer present verbatim ('aliae sunt diuini iuris, aliae humani'); parallels the Book I summa divisio of persons.

pairs.source_text: Diuini iuris sunt ueluti res sacrae et religiosae.
pairs.question: Quae sunt res divini iuris secundum Gaium?
pairs.question_en: What are the things of divine law according to Gaius?
pairs.answer_en: Sacred things (res sacrae) and religious things (res religiosae).
pairs.derivation: Gaius subdivides res divini iuris into res sacrae and res religiosae. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius + res divini iuris, two named-term answer present verbatim ('res sacrae et religiosae').

pairs.source_text: Sacrae sunt, quae diis superis consecratae sunt; religiosae, quae diis Manibus relictae sunt.
pairs.question: Quibus diis res sacrae consecratae et res religiosae relictae sunt secundum Gaium?
pairs.answer: Sacrae diis superis, religiosae diis Manibus.
pairs.question_en: To which gods are sacred things consecrated and religious things left, according to Gaius?
pairs.answer_en: Sacred things to the gods above (dii superi), religious things to the gods of the dead (dii Manes).
pairs.derivation: Gaius's defining distinction between res sacrae (consecrated to the gods above) and res religiosae (left to the di Manes). Closed-book definitional fact, anchored to Gaius, paired named-entity answer present verbatim ('quae diis superis consecratae sunt ... quae diis Manibus relictae sunt').

pairs.source_text: Hae autem res, quae humani iuris sunt, aut publicae sunt aut priuatae.
pairs.question: In quae duo genera res humani iuris dividi Gaius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Into which two kinds does Gaius report that things of human law are divided?
pairs.derivation: Gaius's subdivision of res humani iuris into res publicae and res privatae. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius + res humani iuris, two-part answer present verbatim ('aut publicae sunt aut priuatae'); indirect statement (res dividi) governed by tradit.

pairs.source_text: Corporales hae sunt, quae tangi possunt, uelut fundus, homo, uestis, aurum, argentum et denique aliae res innumerabiles.
pairs.question: Quas res Gaius corporales esse dicit?
pairs.question_en: Which things does Gaius say are corporeal?
pairs.derivation: Gaius's classic definition of res corporales as things that can be touched (opposed to res incorporales). Closed-book jurisprudential definition, anchored to Gaius, short answer present verbatim ('Corporales hae sunt, quae tangi possunt'); indirect statement (res corporales esse) governed by dicit.

pairs.source_text: Res praeterea aut mancipi sunt aut nec mancipi.
pairs.question: In quae duo genera res praeterea dividi Gaius scribit?
pairs.answer: In res mancipi et nec mancipi.
pairs.question_en: Into which two kinds does Gaius write that things are further divided?
pairs.answer_en: Into things mancipi and things nec mancipi.
pairs.derivation: Gaius's famous division of things into res mancipi and res nec mancipi, fundamental to Roman property law. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius, two named-term answer present verbatim ('aut mancipi sunt aut nec mancipi').

pairs.source_text: Sed item fere omnia, quae incorporalia sunt, nec mancipi sunt, exceptis seruitutibus praediorum rusticorum; nam eas mancipi esse constat, quamuis sint ex numero rerum incorporalium.
pairs.question: Quae sola ex rebus incorporalibus res mancipi esse Gaius adfirmat?
pairs.question_en: Which incorporeal things alone does Gaius affirm to be res mancipi?
pairs.derivation: Gaius notes that although nearly all incorporeal things are nec mancipi, rustic praedial servitudes are res mancipi (an instance of the classic res mancipi set). Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, single named-entity answer present verbatim ('exceptis seruitutibus praediorum rusticorum; nam eas mancipi esse constat'); indirect statement (servitutes mancipi esse) governed by adfirmat.

pairs.source_text: Vsucapio autem mobilium quidem rerum anno completur, fundi uero et aedium biennio; et ita lege XII tabularum cautum est.
pairs.question: Quibus temporibus usucapionem rerum mobilium et fundi compleri Gaius scribit?
pairs.question_en: In what periods does Gaius write that usucapion of movable things and of land is completed?
pairs.answer_en: Of movables in one year, of land in two years.
pairs.derivation: Gaius gives the usucapio periods fixed by the Twelve Tables: one year for movables, two years for land and buildings. Closed-book crisp numeric fact, anchored to Gaius + XII Tables, both periods present verbatim ('mobilium quidem rerum anno completur, fundi uero et aedium biennio'); indirect statement (usucapionem compleri) governed by scribit.

pairs.source_text: Praeterea id, quod in solo nostro ab aliquo aedificatum est, quamuis ille suo nomine aedificauerit, iure naturali nostrum fit, quia superficies solo cedit.
pairs.question: Quo principio id quod in solo nostro ab alio aedificatum est nostrum fieri Gaius docet?
pairs.question_en: On what principle does Gaius teach that what another builds on our land becomes ours?
pairs.answer_en: Because the surface yields to the soil (superficies solo cedit).
pairs.derivation: Gaius states the famous maxim superficies solo cedit: what is built on our soil becomes ours by natural law. Closed-book classical legal maxim, anchored to Gaius, short answer present verbatim ('quia superficies solo cedit'); indirect statement (id nostrum fieri) governed by docet.

pairs.source_text: Testamentorum autem genera initio duo fuerunt: nam aut calatis comitiis testamentum faciebant, quae comitia bis in anno testamentis faciendis destinata erant, aut in procinctu, id est, cum belli causa arma sumebant: procinctus est enim expeditus et armatus exercitus. Accessit deinde tertium genus testamenti, quod per aes et libram agitur.
pairs.question: Quae tria genera testamentorum apud Romanos fuisse Gaius commemorat?
pairs.answer: Calatis comitiis, in procinctu, et per aes et libram.
pairs.question_en: Which three kinds of testament does Gaius record existed among the Romans?
pairs.answer_en: In the calate assembly (calatis comitiis), in battle array (in procinctu), and by bronze and balance (per aes et libram).
pairs.derivation: Gaius enumerates the three historical forms of testament: the two original ones (calatis comitiis and in procinctu) and the later per aes et libram. Closed-book famous legal-history fact, anchored to Gaius, three named forms present verbatim across 2.101-102; indirect statement (genera fuisse) governed by commemorat.

pairs.source_text: Heredes autem aut necessarii dicuntur aut sui et necessarii aut extranei.
pairs.question: In quae tria genera heredes dividi Gaius scribit?
pairs.answer: In necessarios, suos et necessarios, et extraneos.
pairs.question_en: Into which three classes does Gaius write that heirs are divided?
pairs.answer_en: Into necessary heirs (necessarii), own-and-necessary heirs (sui et necessarii), and external heirs (extranei).
pairs.derivation: Gaius's threefold classification of heirs: necessarii, sui et necessarii, extranei. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius, three named-term answer present verbatim ('aut necessarii ... aut sui et necessarii aut extranei'); indirect statement (heredes dividi) governed by scribit.

pairs.source_text: Legatorum itaque genera sunt quattuor: aut enim per uindicationem legamus aut per damnationem aut sinendi modo aut per praeceptionem.
pairs.question: Quot sunt legatorum genera secundum Gaium, et quae?
pairs.answer: Quattuor: per vindicationem, per damnationem, sinendi modo, et per praeceptionem.
pairs.question_en: How many kinds of legacy are there according to Gaius, and which?
pairs.answer_en: Four: by vindication (per vindicationem), by condemnation (per damnationem), by permission (sinendi modo), and by preception (per praeceptionem).
pairs.derivation: Gaius's classic fourfold division of legacies with the determinate count. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius, count and four named kinds present verbatim ('genera sunt quattuor: aut enim per uindicationem ... aut per damnationem aut sinendi modo aut per praeceptionem').

pairs.source_text: Lata est itaque lex Falcidia, qua cautum est, ne plus ei legare liceat quam dodrantem: itaque necesse est, ut heres quartam partem hereditatis habeat.
pairs.question: Quam partem hereditatis heredi servari lex Falcidia iubet, ut Gaius scribit?
pairs.question_en: What portion of the inheritance does the lex Falcidia require to be reserved for the heir, as Gaius writes?
pairs.derivation: Gaius records that the lex Falcidia capped legacies at three-quarters (dodrans), guaranteeing the heir a quarter (the Falcidian quarter). Closed-book famous numeric/legal fact, anchored to the named lex Falcidia + Gaius, fraction answer present verbatim ('necesse est, ut heres quartam partem hereditatis habeat').
